Disease Outbreak Disrupts Austrian Machinery Industry Operations

VIENNA, June 13 – A sudden outbreak of norovirus has struck Austria’s machinery industry, forcing temporary closures at several key production sites and causing widespread absenteeism among factory workers, industry sources said Thursday.

The first cases were reported last week at MachinaTech’s facility in Linz, with more than 60 employees affected. Since then, at least six other machinery plants, including those operated by Alpensysteme GmbH and Steirische Maschinenbau AG, have reported clusters of infections. The Austrian Machinery Association said over 400 workers across the sector are currently absent due to illness.

“The rapid spread of the virus has posed significant challenges to our operations,” said Karl Bauer, spokesperson for the association. “Production lines at several sites are running at reduced capacity, and some have had to halt work entirely for deep cleaning and to prevent further transmission.”

The affected companies have implemented enhanced sanitation protocols and staggered shifts, but officials say that maintaining output remains difficult. “We are doing everything possible to protect our workforce and resume normal operations, but the health and safety of our employees is our top priority,” Bauer added.

Union representatives expressed concern about working conditions, noting that many assembly workers operate in close quarters. “We urge all employers to provide paid leave for affected staff and ensure thorough disinfection of all machinery and common areas,” said Petra Leitner, a regional union leader.

Industry analysts estimate that machinery production in Austria could fall by up to 15% this month if the outbreak continues. “With ongoing absenteeism and site closures, the risk of supply bottlenecks within the industry is increasing,” said Michael Gruber, a Vienna-based sector analyst.

Local health authorities are monitoring the situation and have recommended that machinery firms reinforce hygiene measures. As of Thursday, the outbreak remains contained within the industry, but officials caution that continued vigilance is needed to limit further spread.
